success_patterns: Match the option to the exact kind of claim requested: a lower bound on a liminf is not automatically an eventual counting bound with the same exponent and fixed constant; a sufficient condition is not an if-and-only-if criterion; and a two-sided estimate requires both sides.

For near-duplicate options, isolate the changed detail instead of relying on plausibility: signs, factors, index restrictions, divisibility direction, and scopes such as “every” versus “at least one” or “only one” versus “at most one.”

For complete classifications and uniform statements, check both directions, every quantified case, and the full stated parameter range; do not substitute a partial result or a stronger-sounding claim for the one established.

These trajectories repeatedly show that the decisive step is often checking logical strength and endpoint formulations among nearly identical choices, so a short addition can make that comparison more operational without adding theorem-specific facts.

edits.content:
## Check logical strength at the exact endpoint
When options differ mainly in formulation, verify their logical implications rather than treating them as interchangeable: a liminf exponent bound need not give an eventual lower bound with the same exponent and a fixed constant; a sufficient condition is not an iff criterion; and a two-sided estimate requires both bounds. For complete classifications, check necessity and sufficiency and each quantified case. Compare near-identical formulas literally—including signs, factors, index restrictions, and divisibility direction—and distinguish scopes such as “every” versus “at least one” and “only one” versus “at most one” (checking whether existence is already guaranteed). For uniform claims, ensure the stated constants and conclusions hold over the full parameter range.
